planting.note: Tuck divisions directly into dry limestone or dolomite crevices; avoid rich, moist, or acidic planting sites.

directions: Tuck divisions or small container plants into dry, sharply drained crevices of limestone or dolomite outcrops and ledges, in full sun to light shade, where the fronds can root directly into cracks filled with thin, alkaline, rocky soil. Smooth cliffbrake forms low, dense tufts of wiry, straw-colored stipes topped with leathery, blue-green, once- to twice-pinnate fronds that curl tightly in drought and re-expand after rain, a hallmark of this xerophytic calciphile. It is common on the limestone cliffs and ledges of the Ridge and Valley province, where it often grows beside its purple-stiped relative Pellaea atropurpurea but lacks that species' dark stem color. Avoid rich, moist, or acidic soils and any shading by lush neighboring vegetation, both of which cause this fern to decline; it performs best where almost nothing else will grow.

planting.note: Site on open, dry, rocky, alkaline ground; declines in wet, acidic, or heavily organic soil.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into dry to moderately moist, well-drained, distinctly alkaline soil on open rocky slopes, bluffs, or woodland edges in full sun to light shade, mimicking the limestone and dolomite exposures of the Ridge and Valley region where it grows wild. Lanceleaf buckthorn is a native, non-invasive dioecious shrub bearing small, lance-shaped, finely toothed leaves and inconspicuous greenish spring flowers; only pollinated female plants produce the small blue-black drupes that songbirds eat into winter. Unlike the introduced common and glossy buckthorns it does not spread aggressively, making it a sound choice for restoring calcareous woodland edges and rocky hedgerows. Site it where limestone-derived soil stays on the dry side, since it declines in wet, acidic, or heavily organic ground.
sources: Flora of Virginia Project / Virginia Native Plant Society
